dish: Wet-bottom shoofly pie from the original 1946 recipe, served warm with whipped cream
w: Lancaster County's first tourist attraction (1946) and 'the place that made shoo-fly pie famous' — it began serving the molasses-and-crumb pie to Route 30 travelers and shipping it nationwide in the 1950s; TIME once called it America's best. Also a sprawling Amish-country gift shop under the landmark windmill.

dish: PA Dutch smorgasbord — chicken pot pie, schnitz un knepp, carved ham, buttered noodles and a dessert bar of shoofly and whoopie pies
w: The largest buffet in North America: 200 feet of Pennsylvania Dutch cooking serving some 1.2 million diners a year, voted best buffet in the US by USA Today 10Best readers (2024). A pilgrimage in itself — go hungry, go early.

dish: Chicken & waffles (the dish that started it in 1929) and the traditional PA Dutch smorgasbord with shoofly pie
w: A Lancaster County institution since 1929, when it began as a chicken-and-waffles stop for Route 30 motorists; placed third in USA Today 10Best's readers' poll for best buffet. The more traditional, sit-and-linger smorgasbord counterpart to Shady Maple's scale.

dish: Hand-twisted soft and hard pretzels — and a hands-on twisting lesson
w: America's first commercial pretzel bakery, opened in 1861 in an 18th-century Lititz house; the original ovens are still here and every tour ends with you twisting your own. The birthplace of the hard pretzel in the US.

dish: Stall-hop the PA Dutch canon — shoofly and whoopie pies, sweet bologna, chow-chow — plus pierogi, empanadas and soul food
w: Recognized as the oldest continuously operating public farmers market in the US (est. 1730), in an 1889 Romanesque Revival market house off Penn Square. 60-plus standholders; open Tue, Fri and Sat mornings only — go early.

dish: Pennsylvania Dutch stands alongside the city's international food counters — eat your way through both brick and stone market houses
w: Founded in 1860 (it fed Union soldiers at Camp Curtin) and among the oldest continuously operating market houses in the US; on the National Register since 1974. Midtown Harrisburg's anchor, run by the non-profit Broad Street Market Alliance. Thu–Sat only.

dish: Generations-old stands — Henry's Ham, J. L. Miller Meats, Hartman's Fruit Farm — plus a food-hall's worth of lunch counters
w: Downtown York's 1888 John Dempwolf market house, a Romanesque Revival landmark on the National Register since 1978, in continuous operation since it opened; 50-plus vendors, some trading here for more than 70 years.

dish: Lebanon bologna — all-beef, hardwood-smoked for three days in wooden smokehouses — sliced to taste in the outlet
w: Smoking Lebanon bologna since 1902, four generations on; the outlet store and museum lead to hairnet tours of the original wooden smokehouses where a smokemaster tends the fire around the clock. The definitive taste of this region's signature cold cut, minutes from Hershey.

dish: Fresh-off-the-line Utz potato chips after the free self-guided Chip Trip
w: The glass-walled observation gallery above Utz's Hanover plant shows potatoes going from truck to fryer to bag, then deposits you in the factory outlet — the signature stop in the 'Snack Food Capital of the World.'

dish: Snyder's of Hanover pretzels — sourdough hards, pretzel pieces and chocolate-covered — at factory-store prices
w: The factory store of what was once the country's best-selling pretzel brand, born in Hanover's Pennsylvania Dutch snack belt in 1909.

dish: Small-batch ice cream from the farm's own Jersey herd in a fresh waffle cone
w: Working dairy farm whose butterfat-rich small-batch ice cream is a can't-miss Amish-country dessert stop; chosen as the launch site of Pennsylvania's 2026 Scooped Ice Cream Trail.

dish: On-farm ice cream in flavors like meadow tea sorbet, monkey bread and brown-butter almond brickle
w: Family dairy farm turned creamery making hand-crafted ice cream from its own milk; ranked near the top of Lancaster's ice cream surveys.

dish: Tenderloin tips on toast — the Shaub family's Prohibition-era speakeasy dish, still on the menu
w: Lancaster city's oldest continuously operating restaurant: a mid-1800s carriage house whose loft became a 1920s speakeasy. Horse stalls are dining nooks, wagon wheels the chandeliers, and the original entrance still hides down an unnamed alley.

dish: Grandma Smucker's wet-bottom shoofly pie and jumbo whoopie pies, baked from scratch
w: The Smucker family's scratch bakery in the village of Bird-in-Hand; its shoofly pie (a light-syrup, never-bitter take on the molasses classic) starred in Al Roker's 'Family Style' episode on the history of American pie. Whoopie-pie samplers by the dozen.

dish: Colonial fare by candlelight — French onion soup in an iron kettle in the Springhouse Tavern
w: Gettysburg's oldest building (1776), Rev. Alexander Dobbin's home and later an Underground Railroad station, now a National Register-listed restaurant: candlelit fine dining upstairs, the cellar Springhouse Tavern with its springs and fireplaces below.

dish: Civil War-era plates — game pie, peanut soup and spoon bread — served by period-dressed staff
w: An 1810/1833 house whose south wall still carries more than 100 bullet holes from the battle (Confederate sharpshooters used its garret); dine in the Meade and Lee rooms or the casual Sweney's Tavern.

dish: The Half Gallon Challenge — a half-gallon of ice cream in one sitting, the AT thru-hiker's midpoint rite
address: Pine Grove Furnace State Park, Gardners, PA 17324
w: The little store across from the Appalachian Trail Museum where, for 40-plus years, thru-hikers reaching the trail's symbolic halfway point have tried to finish a half-gallon of ice cream; finishers earn a commemorative wooden spoon.

dish: Friday-only feast: PA Dutch baked goods, sweet bologna and fresh-cut fries across 400 stands and an auction
w: A 60-acre Friday institution since 1932 — one of the largest and oldest farmers markets on the East Coast, with 400-plus vendors, a livestock and hay auction, and Amish and Mennonite stands. Voted the No. 2 farmers market in the US by USA Today readers (2021).

dish: Tuesday market-day eating — fresh produce, baked goods and PA Dutch deli across 200 vendors
w: Lancaster County's Tuesday market since the 1920s — older than Green Dragon — with 200-plus vendors, a produce auction and antiques; open year-round.

dish: Hand-rolled PA Dutch pretzels, jams and jellies, and Amish baked goods
w: Family-run indoor market of three-plus decades in the village of Bird-in-Hand — the easy, compact place to shop the county's pretzels, jams, fudge and baked goods.

dish: Pick-your-own apples and blueberries, then cider donuts and fruit pies from the farm market
w: A 500-acre third-generation family farm (since 1955) in the Adams County fruit belt — Pennsylvania's largest apple-growing county; year-round market on PA 34 and a stop on Destination Gettysburg's Crop Hop trail.

dish: Wood-fired Neapolitan-leaning pizzas and handmade pasta from local Lancaster County produce
w: Chef Nathan Flaim's acclaimed Italian restaurant, a 2026 James Beard Award finalist for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic — the city's highest national culinary honor in years.

dish: Farm-to-table plates and house-brewed beer in the rooftop biergarten
w: Midtown Harrisburg's 'Art. Food. Music.' hub since 2015, built from the reclaimed timber of the old Stokes Millwork: a farm-to-table restaurant, brewery and rooftop biergarten over two floors of working artist studios. Named to OpenTable's Top 100 Hot Spot Restaurants in America.

dish: Kettle-style Martin's potato chips, fresh from the free Tuesday factory tour
w: York County family chipmaker in Thomasville since the 1940s; free 45-minute tours run Tuesday mornings by reservation — pair it with Utz and Snyder's in nearby Hanover for the full 'Snack Food Capital' circuit.

dish: Award-winning chocolate peanut-butter stout and the brewery's pumpkin ale
w: Lancaster's inventive brewery, best known for its dessert stouts and pumpkin ales; the taproom is just outside downtown with a second tasting room on West King Street.
